clue.text: Start to pound and batter about the entrance to Ilium, finding its King

indicators.note: the start of the word pound is its opening letter, so only that is taken
the battering word goes about, that is around, the next piece

parts.note: to batter a wall is to ram it

indicators.note: the entrance of the word Ilium is its first letter, the way in

explanation.surface: A siege tale: pounding and battering at the gates of Troy until its king is found.
explanation.walkthrough: P from 'Start to pound'; RAM ('batter') goes 'about' I, the entrance to Ilium. 'its King' points back to Ilium, another name for Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: Priam was the last monarch of Troy in Homer's Iliad, and Ilium is Troy's Greek name.

clue.text: Baroness's colourful hero, the flower of the English

definitions.meaning: Baroness Orczy's hero Sir Percy Blakeney goes by the name of a red wild flower, the Scarlet one
a small scarlet wild flower of English fields and hedgerows

explanation.walkthrough: Baroness Orczy wrote The Scarlet Pimpernel, whose dandy hero rescues aristocrats from the guillotine; 'colourful' hints at scarlet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scarlet Pimpernel is both Orczy's title hero and a red-flowered plant common in England.

clue.text: But it's not what Johnson did when writing his essays!

definitions.text: But it's not what Johnson did when writing his essays!

parts.words: But it's not what Johnson did when writing his essays!
parts.note: Samuel Johnson's periodical essays were called The Idler, yet writing them was work, so he was not loafing about

explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's 1758-60 essay series was The Idler; the clue jokes that the man behind it did the opposite of lazing.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit about doing nothing is the past tense the joke turns on, the verb behind Johnson's title.

clue.text: Traveller turning up, one that's aesthetic, a latter-day Napoleon

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the traveller word from bottom to top

parts.note: a Rom is a Romany traveller
one is the Roman numeral I
arty means having artistic or aesthetic pretensions

explanation.surface: A wandering aesthete is compared to Napoleon in modern times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses ROM to MOR. Sherlock Holmes called Professor Moriarty 'the Napoleon of crime'.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's arch-villain is dubbed the Napoleon of crime, a modern emperor of the underworld.

clue.text: Old Nick's daughter, a first-class devil round about the start of solemnities

indicators.note: the reversed letters go about, that is around, the next piece
turned round, the first-class and devil words are both read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-class, with the figure 1 read as the letter I
Satan is the devil

indicators.note: the start of the word solemnities is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A family tree of Satan: his daughter is a top-rank devil in solemn rites.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' turns AISATAN into NATASIA; S, the start of solemnities, goes inside ('about') to give NASTASIA after A. 'Old Nick' is not the devil but Tsar Nicholas II.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Duchess Anastasia was the youngest daughter of Tsar Nicholas II, the last Russian emperor.

clue.text: Sounds like a bird one met in the great hall at Univ

indicators.note: the solver is told that the bird and the number, said together, match the entry

parts.note: a bird is an owl, and one is A

explanation.surface: Meeting a bird in a college dining hall sounds like an Oxford anecdote.
explanation.walkthrough: OWL and A run together sound like the Latin word for a hall. Univ is the nickname of University College, Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Aula is Latin for a hall or court, used for a university's ceremonial assembly hall.

clue.text: In which to read about Napoleon, the swine!

definitions.text: In which to read about Napoleon, the swine!

parts.words: In which to read about Napoleon, the swine!
parts.note: Orwell's fable has a pig named Napoleon who becomes a tyrant, so the insult 'swine' is literal

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like an outburst against Bonaparte; Orwell's pig ruler is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's 1945 satire features the boar Napoleon seizing power on a farm run by beasts.

clue.text: Commotion about the Spanish turning up in foreign painter's home town

indicators.note: the fuss word goes about, that is around, the next piece

parts.note: a to-do is a fuss or commotion

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the Spanish article from bottom to top

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Some fuss in a foreign painter's home town.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'foreign painter' is El Greco, a Cretan-born Greek who settled in the Castilian city; 'turning up' is the reversal signal for a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco, the Cretan-born painter, made Toledo his home for the rest of his career.

clue.text: In which Miss Bergman suffered from an eruption

definitions.text: In which Miss Bergman suffered from an eruption

parts.words: In which Miss Bergman suffered from an eruption
parts.note: Ingrid Bergman starred in Rossellini's 1950 film named after a volcanic island, and the eruption is the volcano, not a rash

explanation.walkthrough: 'suffered from an eruption' sounds like a skin complaint; it is the volcano in Rossellini's film.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rossellini film starring Ingrid Bergman takes its title from an active volcanic island off Sicily.

clue.text: Divine beings occasionally seen among water-skiers

indicators.note: occasionally means taking only every other letter of the water-skiers

explanation.surface: Gods are sometimes spotted among people on water skis.
explanation.walkthrough: The 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th and 10th letters of WATERSKIERS are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aesir are the principal gods of Norse mythology, such as Odin and Thor.

clue.text: Like Molière's doctor, I'll argue violently with chief of medicine

indicators.note: the chief, the head, of the word medicine is its first letter
the letters of I'll argue are thrown violently about

explanation.surface: A quarrelsome doctor argues angrily with the head of medicine.
explanation.walkthrough: Molière's play Le Médecin malgré lui is about a woodcutter forced to act as a doctor in spite of himself; 'violently' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière's woodcutter is made a physician against his will, a doctor 'in spite of himself', the French phrase.

clue.text: Gods are to be seen in Lesotho

indicators.note: the word are is to be seen in, placed inside, the Lesotho code

parts.note: LS is the international code for Lesotho

explanation.surface: Deities are visible in the southern African kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: Countries have two-letter international codes, and Lesotho's is the pair used here; 'to be seen in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: The lares were Roman household deities guarding the home and family.

clue.text: Reads new second Greco- Latin version of Ezra

indicators.note: a new version of the word reads rearranges its letters

explanation.surface: A scholar reads a fresh second Greek and Latin text of the Book of Ezra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' signals the anagram. The Greek and Latin Bibles give Ezra's name in this form for their apocryphal books.
explanation.definitionFit: Esdras is the Greek and Latin form of Ezra's name, used for the books in the Septuagint and Vulgate.

clue.text: Sick feeling engendered by hearing a poor performance of Debussy?

definitions.meaning: seasickness, the nausea of a sea crossing
read in French as a bad rendering of Debussy's orchestral work La Mer

explanation.walkthrough: In French 'mal' is bad, so a botched La Mer is a 'mal de Mer'; 'engendered by hearing' links the two.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase literally means sickness of the sea, the queasiness of a rough crossing.

clue.text: Subject for Ackroyd to speak to novelist initially

parts.note: to chatter is to speak at length

indicators.note: initially means just the first letter of the word novelist

explanation.surface: An Ackroyd research topic involves talking to a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Ackroyd's 1987 novel is about the boy poet Thomas Chatterton.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Ackroyd made the 18th-century poet Thomas Chatterton the subject of his 1987 novel.

clue.text: "If she had a petticoat over her -, that was all" (Conrad, The Rover)

definitions.text: "If she had a petticoat over her -, that was all" (Conrad, The Rover)

parts.words: "If she had a petticoat over her -, that was all" (Conrad, The Rover)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap, filled by the woman's nightgown in Conrad's novel

explanation.definitionFit: A chemise worn in bed, the garment Conrad describes under a hastily added petticoat.

clue.text: Going up, say, recklessly to greet Miss Heyer

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up reads the abbreviation for say from bottom to top

parts.note: eg (for example) means say

indicators.note: the letters of to greet are tumbled recklessly

explanation.surface: Someone rushes upstairs carelessly to welcome a lady novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going up' reverses EG to GE; 'recklessly' turns TOGREET into ORGETTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgette Heyer was the English author of Regency romances and detective stories.

clue.text: Robert Vaughn in the role of Napoleon

definitions.text: Robert Vaughn in the role of Napoleon

parts.words: Robert Vaughn in the role of Napoleon
parts.note: Vaughn played the spy Napoleon of that surname in The Man from U.N.C.L.E.

explanation.walkthrough: Not Bonaparte: Vaughn's character in the 1960s TV series was the secret agent Napoleon of U.N.C.L.E.
explanation.definitionFit: Vaughn's character in The Man from U.N.C.L.E. was the agent whose surname completes Napoleon.

clue.text: Collections of books which travellers may find useful

definitions.meaning: volumes gathering several works by one author
large public road vehicles carrying passengers

explanation.walkthrough: The plural of the old word for a bus serves both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both anthologies in one volume and passenger buses, from Latin 'for all'.

clue.text: Latter-day Napoleon, a very heartless cat I'm worried about

indicators.note: the letters are worried about, shaken around, to make the cat
heartless removes the middle of the word very, keeping its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A cat is very anxious about a modern-day tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: A, VY (very without its heart) and CATIM are rearranged ('worried about'). In T. S. Eliot's Old Possum poems, Macavity is called the Napoleon of Crime.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot's mystery cat is dubbed the Napoleon of Crime, echoing Holmes's Moriarty.

clue.text: American actor seen in second half of Napoleon

indicators.note: the second half of the word Napoleon is its last four letters

explanation.surface: An American actor appears in the latter part of a Napoleon film.
explanation.walkthrough: The last four letters of NAPOLEON are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Leon Ames was an American film actor; Leon is also a performer's name in its own right.

clue.text: What led to Hamsun's Hunger, or alternatively to variants?

indicators.note: alternatively says the letters of to variants are rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: A question about what caused the hunger in Knut Hamsun's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternatively' rearranges TOVARIANTS. Hunger (1890) is Knut Hamsun's novel of a starving writer in Oslo.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of food to the point of famine is what produces the hunger of Hamsun's narrator.

clue.text: Platform for Upton Sinclair in 19267?

parts.note: Upton Sinclair's 1927 novel is titled Oil!, and a platform for drilling is the joke

explanation.walkthrough: A 'platform' sounds political; Sinclair was a campaigner, but the platform here is offshore drilling, tied to his novel Oil!.
explanation.definitionFit: A drilling platform at sea for extracting petroleum, the subject of Sinclair's novel.

clue.text: Musician to prate about the TLS, say, in East London

indicators.note: turned about, the prattle word is read backwards

parts.note: to gab is to prate or chatter

parts.words: the TLS, say, in East London
parts.note: the TLS is a paper, and in Cockney speech of East London paper is said piper

explanation.surface: A performer chatters about the literary weekly in a Cockney accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses GAB to BAG. Cockneys, the East Londoners, are said to pronounce 'paper' as 'piper'.
explanation.definitionFit: A piper on the Scottish wind instrument with a bag and drones is a kind of musician.

clue.text: Where Kipling's girl was rising in the morning with difficulty

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising reads the whole run from bottom to top

parts.note: am is morning, ante meridiem
a rub is a difficulty, as in Hamlet's there's the rub

explanation.surface: A girl in Kipling gets up in the morning with difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns AMRUB into BURMA. Kipling's poem Mandalay speaks of 'a Burma girl a-settin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Mandalay places its girl in Burma, the country now called Myanmar.

clue.text: Is able to face the bowlers on returning to one side in the Varsity match

definitions.text: one side in the Varsity match

parts.note: can means is able

indicators.note: returning reads the cricket word backwards

parts.note: to bat in cricket is to face the bowlers

explanation.surface: A cricketer who can bat comes back for a university team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns BAT into TAB. The Varsity match is the annual Oxford v Cambridge fixture; a Cantab is a Cambridge man.
explanation.definitionFit: Cantab, short for Cantabrigian, means a member of Cambridge University, one team in the Varsity match.

clue.text: A letter to the erstwhile reservists

parts.note: the TA was the Territorial Army, Britain's former volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A letter is sent to former army reservists.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army was renamed the Army Reserve in 2014, hence 'erstwhile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Creation featuring spice turning up in menu-delicious!

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the concealed run from bottom to top
in says the letters sit inside the words menu-delicious

explanation.surface: A dish with spice turns up on a menu and is delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: ENUD sits inside 'menu-delicious' and 'turning up' reverses it. Frank Herbert's novel centres on the spice melange.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Herbert's science-fiction novel revolves around the spice mined on the desert planet Arrakis.

clue.text: Turner's version of New Zealand city, omitting its University Academy

definitions.note: a turner here is any thing that spins, with 's standing for is

indicators.note: omitting means the letters for university and academy are taken out of the city

parts.note: Rotorua is a city in New Zealand's North Island
U is university and A is academy

explanation.surface: A painter's view of a New Zealand city, leaving out its university.
explanation.walkthrough: The painter J. M. W. Turner is a red herring: the 'turner' is a spinning part of a machine. 'its' links the letters to the end of ROTORUA.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the spinning part of a machine, such as a helicopter's blades, so it is a thing that turns.

clue.text: "On ghosts of servers and — after Mass" (Betjeman)

definitions.text: "On ghosts of servers and — after Mass" (Betjeman)

parts.words: "On ghosts of servers and — after Mass" (Betjeman)
parts.note: a Betjeman line with a gap, filled by the altar attendants who carry censers

explanation.definitionFit: Altar servers who swing the censer of incense at Mass, as Betjeman's line recalls.

clue.text: Director of Napoléon has a beautiful French look, sans un soupçon de la laideur

annotationWithheld.why: "Director of Napoléon has a beautiful French look, sans un soupçon de la laideur": A + BEL (beautiful French) is clear, but no reading of 'look, sans un soupçon de la laideur' gives GANCE
annotationWithheld.clue: Director of Napoléon has a beautiful French look, sans un soupçon de la laideur

clue.text: "Napoleon was never of his own time" (-, The Trembling of the Veil)

definitions.text: "Napoleon was never of his own time" (-, The Trembling of the Veil)

parts.words: "Napoleon was never of his own time" (-, The Trembling of the Veil)
parts.note: a quotation with its author left blank, from an Irish poet's autobiographical volume

explanation.definitionFit: The Trembling of the Veil (1922) is the Irish poet W. B.'s memoir of his early years.
